planting.note: Divide established crowns or plant nursery divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a named clonal fern selection, propagated by division rather than spores to remain true to type.

directions: Divide established crowns or plant nursery divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in partial to full shade. This slender selection of the golden-scaled male fern carries the same warm rust-orange scaling on emerging croziers as the species, but its fronds are noticeably narrower than 'Cristata The King' and each frond tip and pinna forks into a neat, compact crest rather than a broad tassel, giving the whole plant a more refined, upright silhouette. It stays substantially evergreen through mild winters and holds its crested form best on vigorous, well-fed plants growing in consistently moist humus. Site it as an accent among broader-leaved shade perennials, where its narrow crested outline reads as a distinct textural note rather than being lost among bulkier ferns.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a compact, slow-growing named selection best sited where its congested, crimped texture can be viewed up close.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. This dwarf, densely congested sport of the golden-scaled male fern packs tightly overlapping, crisped and ruffled pinnae onto much shorter fronds than the species, producing a compact, textured tuft instead of the tall vase-shaped clump typical of Dryopteris affinis. New croziers emerge clothed in the same warm rust-orange scales that distinguish the species, but unfurl into markedly narrower, more crimped foliage. It is substantially evergreen in mild winters and, because of its diminutive scale, is easily overwhelmed by vigorous neighbors, so give it uncontested space at the front of a shaded bed or in a trough planting.

planting.note: Plant nursery divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a heavily crested heirloom selection propagated by division to preserve its distinctive frond form.

directions: Plant nursery divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. One of the most elaborately crested of the historic golden-scaled male fern selections, this named clone produces a formal, upright shuttlecock of fronds in which the main tip and each pinna repeatedly forks into multiple narrow, finger-like divisions, giving a denser, more heavily tasseled crest than the more common 'Cristata' forms. New growth emerges thickly clothed in warm rust-orange scales that persist along the stipes into summer. It remains substantially evergreen in mild winters and performs best as an anchor specimen where its bold, ornate texture can be appreciated at close range, such as along a shaded path or beside a bench.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; more drought-tolerant once established than most ferns, suiting it to dry shade under mature trees.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. This named clonal selection of the golden-scaled male fern is grown for its refined, uncrested form: narrower, more tapering fronds and finer-textured pinnae than the species, arranged in the same tidy, upright shuttlecock habit. Croziers unfurl in spring clothed in the warm rust-orange scaling characteristic of Dryopteris affinis, mellowing to deep green as fronds mature and remaining substantially evergreen through mild winters. Like the species it tolerates drier shade than most ferns once established, making it a reliable, long-lived choice for the base of large trees where irrigation is inconsistent. Divide congested multi-crowned clumps in early spring only when vigor declines.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; one of the classic Victorian-era lady fern sports, propagated by division to remain true to type.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Discovered during the height of the Victorian fern-collecting craze, this heirloom lady fern selection carries the same soft, twice-cut deciduous fronds as the species but with each pinna further and more finely subdivided, giving the whole frond a delicate, lacy texture distinct from the plain wild form. Its arching habit and bright green spring growth make it a graceful companion for hostas and hardy geraniums in the shade border. Fronds die back cleanly with the first hard frost and re-emerge as tightly coiled fiddleheads the following spring; divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain frond quality.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from drying wind; among the most finely dissected of the historic lady fern selections.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from drying wind. This plumose lady fern selection takes frond dissection further than the species, with pinnae repeatedly and finely divided into a soft, feathery, almost three-dimensional texture that catches light differently than the flatter fronds of the wild form or of 'Vernoniae'. New fiddleheads emerge bright green in spring, mature to a soft mid-green through summer, and die back completely with the first hard frost. Because the finely cut fronds are more prone to wind damage and rapid moisture loss than the plain species, site it in a sheltered, humid corner of the woodland garden rather than an exposed bed. Divide in early spring only when clumps become congested.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; tolerates dry shade once established, like the species.

directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. A historic male fern sport distinguished by heavy, terminal tasseled crests at both the main frond tip and the tips of the individual pinnae, giving each lance-shaped, semi-evergreen frond a distinctly bold, ornamental fringed outline compared to the tapering fronds of the species. It shares the toughness and adaptability that make male fern such a reliable garden plant, tolerating dry shade, poor soil, and periods of neglect better than most crested fern selections. New croziers unfurl already showing the characteristic crest formation in spring; cut back tattered old fronds in late winter just before new growth emerges. Divide congested clumps every five to seven years.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a long-cultivated heirloom selection propagated by division to remain true to type.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade. One of the oldest documented soft shield fern selections, this cultivar produces narrower, more sharply pointed and acutely lobed pinnae than the species, giving each arching, twice-cut frond a crisper, more finely tailored outline. It forms the same trunk-like base of persistent old fronds as the species, which should be left in place through winter to insulate the crown and protect emerging fiddleheads from cold snaps. Evergreen to semi-evergreen depending on winter severity, it is a reliable, slow-spreading specimen for a shaded border or woodland path edge. Remove only the most tattered fronds in late winter, just before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind; a distinct named clone within the Divisilobum Group, propagated by division.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind. This named clone of the Divisilobum Group carries the same lacy, three-dimensional, plumose dissection as 'Herrenhausen' but with a distinctly broader, more overlapping arrangement of the finely cut pinnules, giving the fronds an even denser, more textured appearance up close. Like other Divisilobum selections it is sterile and must be increased by division, which has kept it a comparatively uncommon collector's fern despite more than a century in cultivation. It is evergreen to semi-evergreen and benefits from leaving the persistent old fronds in place over winter to protect the crown. Site it where its intricate texture can be viewed at close range, such as along a shaded path.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tolerates coastal salt spray, dry shade, and heat better than most ferns.

directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. A dwarf, densely tufted selection of holly fern that reaches only a fraction of the height of the species, producing the same glossy, leathery, holly-like pinnae in a tight rosette suited to small containers, shaded rock gardens, or the front edge of a foundation planting where standard holly fern would be too large. It shares the species' unusual toughness for a fern, handling coastal salt spray, urban heat, and drier shade than most ferns tolerate, while remaining evergreen through mild winters. Groom out tattered fronds in late winter and divide congested clumps in spring only occasionally, as this compact form is naturally slow to spread.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade with high humidity; grow as a container or houseplant outside zones 10-12.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade with high humidity. One of the oldest and most celebrated maidenhair fern selections, prized for pinnules so finely and repeatedly cut that the fronds take on an almost thread-like, hair-fine texture unlike any other Adiantum raddianum cultivar, carried on the same glossy black wiry stems as the species. It demands the same steady moisture and humid air as the species and will brown quickly in dry air, direct sun, or drafts. Outdoors it survives only in sheltered, humid zone 10-12 gardens; elsewhere it is best grown as a treasured houseplant or shaded patio specimen, misted regularly. Divide crowded clumps in spring as roots fill the pot.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade with high humidity; grow as a container or houseplant outside zones 10-12.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade with high humidity. This compact, bushy maidenhair selection produces densely overlapping, ruffled pinnae that give the fronds a fuller, more textured appearance than the airier species, making it a popular choice for hanging baskets and dish gardens as well as shaded outdoor containers. It shares the species' need for constant moisture and humid, draft-free air, browning quickly if the potting mix dries out or humidity drops. Grown outdoors only in sheltered, humid zone 10-12 sites, it is otherwise best treated as a houseplant or shaded porch specimen, misted regularly and kept away from heat vents. Divide and repot congested clumps in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; a compact sport of the tatting fern, best sited in troughs or the front edge of a shaded bed.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. A dwarf form of the celebrated 'Frizelliae' tatting fern, this compact sport retains the same tightly rounded, bead-like pinnae stacked along a narrow midrib that give the parent cultivar its distinctive knitted or crocheted appearance, but scaled down to only a fraction of the size. Its miniature stature suits shaded troughs, rockeries, and the front edge of a woodland bed where the full-sized 'Frizelliae' would be out of proportion. Deciduous fronds emerge bright green in spring and die back completely with the first hard frost; divide sparingly, as clumps increase slowly.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; green trillium is a Midwestern sessile species of rich bottomland and bluff woods in Missouri, Illinois, and adjacent states.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade. Green trillium is a distinct sessile-flowered species of rich, calcareous bottomland and bluff woods across the lower Midwest, best identified by its narrow, mottled leaves and an upright, stalkless flower whose slender, twisted petals stay entirely apple-green to yellow-green rather than aging toward maroon or bronze like most sessile trilliums. It emerges in early to mid spring alongside other woodland ephemerals and goes fully dormant by midsummer as the canopy closes overhead, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant rhizome. Give it the same rich, humus-laden, seasonally moist but well-drained soil it favors on wooded bluffs, and avoid summer irrigation once the foliage yellows. Established colonies are extremely long-lived but slow to divide, so purchase only nursery-propagated stock and expect gradual increase over many years.
